claims.statement: Artificial languages' degree of naturalness (share of quasi-natural quantifiers: generalized existential, intersective or proportional) correlates with optimality, Pearson r = 0.2516 (bootstrap CI 0.2444-0.2589), so efficient communication can explain the typology of quantifiers.
claims.scope: No attested language inventories: 80,000 artificial languages of 1-10 quantifiers, each a mix of quantifiers from a fixed quasi-natural pool and random quantifiers of formula length <= 12; models up to size 10 collapsed to cardinality tuples (Quantity assumed); uniform need over 286 models; frontier by a 100-generation GA plus interpolation.

quantities.baseline: random non-natural 0.0710; fully conservative 0.0684; fully monotone 0.0597; monotone+conservative 0.0563; quasi-natural 0.0514 -- the two universals alone cover 75% of the random-to-quasi-natural gap

our_assessment.why: Reproduces exactly from the shared tables, and my re-implementation reproduces the authors' informativeness to 2e-13. The correlation is real, and within language size it is larger (0.44). But 'naturalness' here is membership in a pool of 101 quantifiers that are much shorter formulas than the random alternatives (complexity 0.60 vs 0.95), and the comparison never asks what a quantifier needs besides being simple and well-behaved. Matched on complexity, non-natural quantifiers that are fully monotone and conservative make languages that are closer to the frontier and more informative than quasi-natural ones. So the naturalness effect is simplicity plus the universals, with nothing left that is specific to the attested classes. Weighting check (see denic2022#c1, where an ordering flipped with the axis weights): the matched comparison is weighting-free, because complexity is identical by construction (difference 0.000000) and the monotone+conservative languages win on cost alone, so they weakly Pareto-dominate on average. The unmatched ladder (the '75%') is a Euclidean distance and IS weighting-dependent; cite the matched result, not the ladder share. There are also no attested languages: the 'typology' is a theory of which quantifiers are natural, not data on inventories, which the author says plainly (6.3).

claims.statement: In a random sample of languages, neither the degree of monotonicity (r = -0.0590, CI -0.0746 to -0.0426) nor of conservativity (r = 0.0725, CI 0.0565 to 0.0883) nor their product (r = 0.0337, CI 0.0171 to 0.0500) is significantly correlated with optimality.
claims.scope: 20,000 random languages, 2,000 per size 1-10, pooled into one Pearson correlation; degrees are normalised mutual-information measures averaged over a language's quantifiers.

quantities.baseline: mean within-size r = +0.173 (CI 0.160-0.189); per size from -0.214 (1 quantifier) to +0.570 (9 quantifiers)

quantities.name: pearson_r_conservativity_optimality_pooled
quantities.baseline: positive in every size stratum (0.064-0.188); mean within-size r = +0.108

our_assessment.why: Three separate problems, each on the authors' own files. (1) The text says 'not significantly correlated', but every printed bootstrap CI excludes zero; the correlations are small and significant, and monotonicity's is significantly negative. (2) The single correlation pools languages of 1 to 10 quantifiers. Size sets both the optimality band and the spread of a mean-of-n degree, so the pooled r averages strata of opposite sign. For monotonicity, r is negative for 1-4 quantifiers and +0.29 to +0.57 for 6-10; conservativity is positive in every stratum. (3) The same analysis script computes the degree correlations on the Experiment-1 sample, where they are 0.19 / 0.23 / 0.27, about as large as the headline naturalness correlation (0.25). The paper reports only the random-sample ones. And the direct test, comparing languages made of quantifiers that HAVE the universals with ones that do not, shows the universals doing most of the work (c1 ladder). The random sample almost never contains such quantifiers: 2.6% of languages have even one fully monotone and conservative quantifier, so it cannot answer the question. The author's own caveat (5.4) points at this; the reanalysis says it is decisive, not a footnote.

claims.statement: Taken together, the results suggest that semantic universals for quantifiers may be epiphenomenal: a by-product of the pressure for efficient communication that does not need independent explanation.
claims.scope: Stated as a conjecture the results 'suggest, but by no means force' (6.1).

our_assessment.why: The conjecture rests on c2's null, which does not survive (see c2). On the evidence here the inference runs the other way: with complexity matched, the universals by themselves give languages that are at least as efficient as the 'natural' ones. So efficiency is what monotonicity and conservativity deliver, not something that merely co-occurs with them. That is consistent with the universals being explained BY efficiency, which is a different claim from their being epiphenomenal to it. It is also consistent with the same result in two other domains (colour convexity, indefinite non-overlap): a structural constraint carries most of the measured efficiency.

datasheet.caveats: Python pickles (dill); unpickling the meanings needs only numpy, but the languages/expressions pickles need the repo's siminf package on PYTHONPATH. natural_expression_indices has 114 entries for 101 distinct quantifiers.

relations.why: Both from the same group and programme. Denic et al. read the universal (Haspelmath's map) as SUPPORTING efficiency; this paper reads its own null as showing universals are epiphenomenal and cites Denic's smaller universal effect as consistent. Reanalysed, both domains point the same way: structural constraints carry most of the efficiency.

Closeness to an estimated optimum read as evidence for a communicative pressure without a structurally minimal null. Here the structural null is the paper's own universals, and it delivers the efficiency.

open_questions: Why is monotonicity negatively related to optimality in languages of 1-4 quantifiers? A guess to test: a single monotone quantifier is true in about half the models and is uninformative alone, but monotone quantifiers tile the space well together. Check informativeness of monotone vs non-monotone singletons at matched complexity.
Does the structural-null result survive without the Quantity assumption (Reference [66] measured simplicity without it)?

The GA frontier is an estimate: 7 of 80,000 authors' languages and 0.1-0.2% of mine fall below it. Small here, but the indefinites frontier from the same method was far from the exact one -- worth checking how far this one is with a longer or seeded search.
